**The landing line** (ten seconds): short, warm, addressed to both of them, glasses up. 'To Danny and Priya — may you always be each other's second car.' A callback like that gives the room a line to applaud and remember.

Safety rules: no exes, no drinking stories that need context, no joke whose target is the bride, nothing you would not say with his grandmother in the front row — she is. Test the whole thing on one honest friend and cut anything they hesitate at. Boring is survivable at a wedding; a roast that lands wrong is not. Aim for the toast people describe afterward as 'short and it sounded like him.'

Read obit-facts.txt — these are the facts my family gave me for my uncle's obituary. The funeral home's version sounds like a stranger. Can you show me how the same facts become a person, without inventing anything?

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: Walter J. Kaminski, 81, of Millfield. Born March 3, 1944, in Millfield, son of the late Joseph and Anna Kaminski. Survived by his sister, Ruth Kaminski of Millfield; his niece, Carol Bennett; and his nephew, David Kaminski. Worked 38 years as a machinist at Halbrook Tool & Die. Member of St. Stanislaus Parish. Served in the U.S. Army, 1963-1966. Enjoyed fishing.

Your constraint — invent nothing — is exactly right, and it is not the obstacle it feels like. The funeral-home version is flat not because the facts are thin but because they are arranged as a form. Arrangement, emphasis, and one licensed sentence of characterization-from-evidence can make the same facts breathe:

'Walter J. Kaminski, 81, of Millfield, died [date/place — add from your notice]. He was born March 3, 1944, in Millfield, to Joseph and Anna Kaminski, and he never really left: he served in the U.S. Army from 1963 to 1966, came home, and spent 38 years as a machinist at Halbrook Tool & Die, working within a few miles of the house he was born in. He was a member of St. Stanislaus Parish. He enjoyed fishing — the one place, his family says, where a man who fixed things for a living was content to sit still and let something not be fixed.

He is survived by his sister, Ruth Kaminski of Millfield; his niece, Carol Bennett; and his nephew, David Kaminski.'

Audit what I did, because you must be able to defend every word: 'he never really left' is drawn from the facts themselves (born in Millfield, worked in Millfield, survived by family in Millfield) — it is arrangement, not invention. The Army is given its dates. The 38 years are kept whole, because 38 years is a fact with weight. The fishing sentence is the only flourish, and note its construction: 'his family says' — that is the honest frame. If your family would NOT say it, cut the sentence; the obituary still stands, plainer but true.

What I did NOT do: give him a personality trait with no source (no 'beloved,' no 'devoted,' no hobbies beyond the one listed), no cause of death speculation, no invented scenes. An obituary earns its humanity from selection and order, not decoration. If the family can supply ONE more fact — the lake he fished, the thing he machined that the town still uses — add it in place of my flourish. One real detail from his life will do more than any sentence of mine.

My business failed last year. I want to write about it while it's still tender — in a year I'll have a tidy narrative and I don't trust tidy. But right now every draft is either raw venting or a fake-inspirational LinkedIn post. How do I write it honestly in the middle?

You have named the two failure modes precisely: venting (all feeling, no structure — the reader is asked to hold your pain) and the LinkedIn arc (all structure, no feeling — the reader is asked to applaud your growth). Writing honestly in the middle means structure in service of the untidy truth. Some working principles:

**Write in scenes, not verdicts.** The venting and the inspiration both live in verdicts ('I was betrayed by circumstances,' 'failure is the greatest teacher'). The honest middle lives in particulars: the last inventory count, the conversation with your one employee, the sign coming down, what you did the following Monday at 9 a.m. with no office to go to. Scenes cannot be fake-inspirational. They can only be accurate.

**Keep the unresolved parts unresolved on the page.** You are allowed sentences like: 'I still do not know whether closing in March instead of June would have saved it. I have stopped needing to know, most days.' That 'most days' is the sound of honesty. The tidy narrative deletes it; the raw vent cannot achieve it.

**Let the lessons be small and priced.** Not 'I learned resilience' but 'I learned that I will sign a personal guarantee again only with my eyes open, because now I know what the words weigh.' Small lessons with costs attached are believable. Large free ones are not.

**Give the draft a cooling rule.** Write the tender version now — you are right that this access expires. Then wait two weeks before revising, and revise with one question: is this sentence here for the reader, or is it here to make me feel accompanied? Cut the second kind to a private journal, where it belongs and does real work.

The piece you are describing — written from inside the weather, structured like it was written after — is the rarest kind of failure writing there is. It is worth the discipline it demands.
I have to write a toast for my parents' 50th anniversary. Everything I draft sounds like a greeting card. What do I actually know that a card doesn't?

You know the marriage from inside the house, which no card does. Cards know about love in general; you know about Tuesday. Build the toast from the evidence only a child of the marriage has:

**The small systems.** How they divide the world: who drives, who navigates, who kills the spiders, who remembers the birthdays, whose job it is to say 'we should go' at parties. Fifty years is not a feeling — it is a set of systems that never quite broke down. Naming three of them, affectionately, is funnier and more moving than any tribute to devotion.

**One hard season, handled lightly.** Every fifty-year marriage has one, and the room knows it. You do not tell the story — you touch it and move on: 'There were years that were not easy, and they are not the years anyone talks about, because my parents handled them the way they handle everything: privately, and together, and with more humor than the situation deserved.' One sentence of acknowledgment makes the celebration honest instead of airbrushed.

**The thing they still do.** Not what they did — what persists: he still makes her tea first, she still saves him the corner piece. Present tense is where fifty years becomes astonishing: it is not that they lasted; it is that the small machinery of tenderness is still running.

**The landing.** Address it to them, not the room, and keep it to one line: 'To Mom and Dad — thank you for making it look, from the inside, like something a person could actually do.' Then stop. The card versions fail because they praise an abstraction. You were there for the Tuesdays. Toast the Tuesdays.

My dad is dying and he asked me to help him write letters to his grandchildren — they're 6, 9, and 14 — to be opened later. I don't know how to help him do this without it becoming unbearable or fake-cheerful. Talk me through it.

First: what he is asking for is one of the great uses of writing, and your job is not to write the letters — it is to make the writing easy enough that his actual voice gets onto the page. Practical method, tested by many families in exactly your position:

**Short sessions, his words, your hands.** Twenty minutes at a time, you as scribe. Ask him questions and transcribe what he says with minimal editing — his phrases, his jokes, his way of starting sentences. A letter in his syntax, typed by you, is his letter. Resist improving it; the grandchildren will want HIM, not a polished version.

**One letter per child, built from three ingredients.** (1) A specific memory of THAT child — the day at the lake with the six-year-old, what the nine-year-old said about dinosaurs, the fourteen-year-old's actual talent he noticed. Specificity is what makes a letter from the dead feel like presence rather than a message in a bottle. (2) One thing he admires in them, stated plainly. (3) One piece of grandfather-knowledge, small enough to keep: how to tell if a melon is ripe, what to do when you are the new kid, the rule about lending tools. Small true things age better than philosophy.

**On tone:** do not steer him away from sadness and do not let anyone steer him toward fake cheer. The honest register of these letters is usually matter-of-fact love: 'I am sorry I will miss the middle part. Here is what I would have said at your graduation, more or less.' If he jokes, keep the jokes — grandchildren treasure evidence that he was funny more than evidence that he was brave.

**On the unbearable part:** it will be, in stretches, and that is not a sign of failure. Work in short sessions. Let him stop mid-letter; a fragment in his voice is worth more than a completed letter in yours. Write the fourteen-year-old's letter first if he tires — that child will read it soonest and remember him most clearly, and the letter can carry a little more.

When a letter is done, read it back to him aloud. Let him correct it. Then seal it, label it plainly — name, occasion, his name — and put it somewhere the family will actually find. You are not helping him say goodbye in the abstract. You are helping him be present at specific future moments. That is a task with edges, and tasks with edges are survivable.

In retirement-speech.txt is my draft speech for my boss's retirement after 31 years. It's respectful but generic and I have to give it Friday. The facts about her are in the draft — can you show me the revision using only what's there?

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: Margaret has been a pillar of this department for 31 years. She started in the mailroom in 1994 and rose through the ranks through hard work and dedication. She has been a mentor to many and a leader to all. Her institutional knowledge is irreplaceable. Among her many accomplishments, she personally reviewed every single expense report in this department for over two decades, and she ran the office through the flood of 2011 when we worked from the cafeteria for a month. We will miss her wisdom and her presence.

Your draft has a classic problem: the generic sentences are in the front and the GOLD is in the back, treated as decoration. Buried in your own text are two facts that no template contains — she personally reviewed every expense report for over twenty years, and she ran the office from a cafeteria for a month during a flood. A whole career's character is in those two facts: the rigor and the refusal to stop. The revision is mostly promotion:

'Margaret started in the mailroom in 1994. I want to tell you what 31 years actually looked like from the inside. For more than twenty years, every expense report in this department crossed her desk — every one. If you ever wondered why our audits were clean enough to be boring, that is why. And in 2011, when the flood took the office, Margaret ran this department from the cafeteria for a month. The work never stopped. Most of us did not even lose a day, because she had already decided we wouldn't.

People will tell you her knowledge is irreplaceable, and for once the cliché is a plain fact: she is the only person alive who knows why half our procedures exist. Margaret — we are going to find out what you carried by feeling its weight. Thank you for carrying it so well, for so long, that we never noticed it was heavy.'

What I changed, using only your material: 'pillar,' 'rose through the ranks,' 'mentor to many, leader to all' — cut; they are the phrases every retirement speech has, so they say nothing about HER. The mailroom stays, because mailroom-to-31-years is a story in one line. The two buried facts now carry the middle. And the closing converts your weakest line — 'we will miss her wisdom and her presence' — into the same thought with the mechanism shown: you will feel what she carried by its absence.

Deliver it at the speed of the cafeteria sentence. That is the one they will remember.
I keep a folder of rejection letters from literary magazines — 34 of them. I want to write a piece about them that isn't bitter and isn't falsely upbeat. Is there a way in?

There is, and the number is your way in: thirty-four is specific, countable, and faintly comic — it has the makings of a piece that treats rejection as data rather than verdict. The tone you want — neither bitter nor falsely upbeat — is the tone of a person reporting on a long experiment. Structure it like one:

**Open with the taxonomy.** Rejections come in species and you are now an expert: the form letter ('not right for us at this time'), the form letter with one handwritten line (the aristocracy of rejection), the encouraging rejection ('we argued about this one'), the silence that is its own answer after eleven months. Sorting them is funny and true, and it establishes your authority: this is a connoisseur speaking, not a victim.

**The middle is what the folder actually taught you, itemized without inflation.** That the same story drew 'beautifully written, not for us' and a form letter in the same month, which teaches you about taste, not quality. That rejection number nine hurt more than twenty-nine, and why. That you kept the handwritten ones in a different part of the folder — say where. Small, priced observations, like a naturalist's notes.

**End on the folder itself, in the present.** Where it lives, whether it is still growing, what you do when a new one arrives. 'I file them in the blue folder, behind the acceptances — all three of them, in the front, where I can reach them faster.' A line like that (use your real details) is neither bitter nor upbeat. It is something better: it is undefeated without claiming victory, which is the exact emotional truth of a writer who is still going.

What do I do when the person I'm writing about is alive and will read it — and the truthful version is not flattering? Specifically my father, in my memoir. I don't want to wound him and I don't want to lie.

This is the central ethical problem of memoir, and it has no solution that makes it comfortable — but it has disciplines that make it defensible. Work through them in order:

**1. Distinguish your experience from his character.** 'When I was twelve, my father missed my recital because he was working, and I decided that year that his job mattered more than I did' is your experience — unimpeachable, and notably it reports YOUR conclusion, not his motive. 'My father did not care about my childhood' is a verdict on his soul, which you are not qualified to issue and he cannot answer from inside your book. Write the first kind. The reader will draw conclusions; conclusions readers draw themselves are both more powerful and more fair.

**2. Put your own flaws on the same page.** A memoir in which the writer is the only reliable narrator of everyone else's failures reads as prosecution. If the chapter shows your father's absences, let it also show what you misunderstood, what you learned later, what it cost him that you could not see at twelve. This is not balance-as-politeness; it is accuracy. He was a whole person in the events, not a function in your story.

**3. Check facts with him, not interpretations.** Dates, sequences, what was said — ask, and correct what you get wrong. You are not asking permission for your memories. But factual care is the ground your right to interpret stands on.

**4. Give him the courtesy of reading it before strangers do** — not for veto, but so that the first time he meets himself in your pages is not at a bookstore. Many writers find the conversation this forces is the one the memoir was trying to have all along.

**5. Accept the residue.** Even done perfectly, he may be hurt. The question is whether the piece needed to exist and whether you wrote it as fairly as you knew how. Memoirists who wait for a version that wounds no one and lies about nothing usually write nothing. Write the fair version. Fair is achievable. Harmless is not, and chasing it produces the lying you wanted to avoid.

Last one. I have been writing my family's story for three years — immigration, the shop, the house, all of it. I am near the end and I keep avoiding the final chapter. It's about my mother's death and what happened to the family after. Everything else I wrote with love. This chapter I have to write with something else and I don't know what it is.

What you are avoiding is not a chapter — it is the discovery that the book changes genre at the end. Everything before was written with love because love was the truth of it. The last chapter's truth is different, and the something-else you are reaching for has a name: it is written with loyalty to what actually happened, including the parts where love was not enough, or not evenly distributed, or not what people did with their grief.

A few things that help writers through exactly this chapter:

**Let the structure carry you.** You do not have to feel your way through this one sentence by sentence. Decide the chapter's skeleton cold: the death in plain sequence, the funeral as the family performed it, the shop and the house as problems to be solved, the first holiday after. A skeleton is a handrail. Grief writing fails when the writer asks emotion to do the organizing; here, chronology and the plain order of events will hold the weight while you put down facts.

**Write the unsayable sentences in their plainest form.** Whatever the family did after — the argument about the house, the sibling who stopped calling, the thing said at the funeral lunch — write it as flatly as a deposition: who, what, when. Flat is not cold. Flat is respectful of the reader and of the people, because it refuses to perform feelings about them. Your earlier chapters could afford music. This one earns its power from restraint.

**Include your own conduct.** The final chapter of a family story is where the narrator most wants to be invisible, standing outside the aftermath observing. You were in it. What you did — the calls you made or did not make — belongs in the record, at the same flat standard. The chapter's authority comes from the writer not exempting herself.

**And accept what the ending of such a book actually is.** It is not resolution; families do not resolve. It is the moment the story you can tell runs out and the living continues off the page. Many writers find the last line is something small and present-tense — the shop's sign in someone's garage, the recipe card in a new kitchen, a grandchild with her name. The family story does not conclude. It hands off.

Write the skeleton this week. Write the flat sentences next. You have been practicing for this chapter for three years — every scene you wrote with love taught you the family's faces well enough to write this one with accuracy, which is love's harder form.
